title: Koalas Are Getting a Vaccine to Help With Their STD Problem
gist: Chlamydia, likely introduced partly from domestic livestock, has driven koala endangerment across several Australian states; a decade-long wild vaccination program cut infection incidence by three-quarters and boosted reproduction.

themes.theme: Disease as the binding constraint on koala recovery

insights.claim: Sexually transmitted disease, not habitat loss alone, is the survival challenge that has caused koala endangerment in several Australian states as the species reoccupies portions of its former range.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Conservation spending aimed only at land protection can miss the actual limiting factor; veterinary intervention is the higher-leverage line item for this species.
insights.locator: koalas have encountered a new survival challenge

insights.claim: In 2020, 70 percent of koalas arriving at a wildlife hospital in Currumbin, Queensland had chlamydia infections, according to Queensland University of Technology veterinary scientists.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A 70 percent infection rate in presenting animals quantifies the scale of the epidemic and justifies population-level rather than case-by-case treatment.
insights.quote: In 2020, 70 percent of koalas landing in a wildlife hospital in Currumbin, a suburb in Queensland, had chlamydia infections

insights.claim: Koala chlamydia is thought to have spread at least in part from domestic livestock and causes blindness, infertility, and premature death.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A livestock-to-wildlife spillover pathway ties agricultural land use directly to endangered-species outcomes, a live issue for biodiversity-linked land regulation.
insights.locator: Chlamydia, thought to have spread in koalas

insights.claim: A decade-long program of vaccine development and administration to hundreds of wild koalas reduced chlamydia incidence by three-quarters and produced a significant reproductive boost.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A 75 percent incidence reduction is a rare hard efficacy number in wildlife conservation and sets a benchmark for funding similar veterinary programs.
insights.quote: reduced the incidence of chlamydia by three-quarters, giving them a significant reproductive boost
insights.locator: Thankfully, a concerted program of vaccine development

insights.claim: The koala vaccination protocol required capturing each wild animal once for the first dose and recapturing it a month later for a booster.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Two-capture protocols make cost per animal the scaling bottleneck, so single-dose or oral-delivery formulations would be the step-change worth watching.
insights.quote: Each wild-caught koala was captured for a first vaccine, then recaptured a month later for a booster.

insights.claim: Koalas survived severe population bottlenecks during the Pleistocene, which makes their continued existence precarious even before modern disease pressure.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Low ancestral genetic diversity amplifies the impact of any single pathogen, meaning disease shocks in this species compound faster than in genetically diverse populations.
insights.locator: The fact that koalas are still on Earth
